sections.title: Regulated Data And Privacy
sections.content:
Not all data carries the same protection requirements. Several categories of data are governed by specific regulations that define how they must be handled, stored, and disclosed.
PII â€” Personally Identifiable Information: any data that can identify a specific individual. Name, home address, phone number, email address, date of birth, Social Security number, financial account information. PII is the broadest regulated data category. It must be protected from unauthorized access, properly secured in transit and at rest, and disposed of properly. State breach notification laws require organizations to notify affected individuals when PII is exposed in a security incident.
PCI-DSS â€” Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: the security standard governing credit card, debit card, and payment card data. Organizations that store, process, or transmit cardholder data â€” card numbers, CVV codes, expiration dates â€” must comply with PCI-DSS requirements. These include encryption of cardholder data, network segmentation, access controls, and regular security testing. Non-compliance results in financial penalties from the card brands and potential loss of the ability to accept card payments.
HIPAA â€” Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act: governs Protected Health Information â€” PHI â€” in the healthcare industry. PHI includes medical records, diagnoses, treatment information, prescription data, and any health information linked to an identifiable individual. HIPAA requires strict access controls, encryption, audit logging, and business associate agreements with any third party that handles PHI. Breaches require notification to affected individuals and the Department of Health and Human Services, with specific timing requirements.
Government-issued identification information: Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, passport numbers. These identifiers are the primary tools used in identity theft. They require elevated protection and are subject to specific state and federal breach notification requirements.
Data retention: regulations and business policies define how long specific data types must be retained. Financial records: typically seven years. Medical records: varies by state â€” typically seven to ten years. Employee records: varies by jurisdiction. Organizations must balance retention requirements against storage costs and privacy obligations â€” retaining data beyond its required period creates unnecessary risk.
Acceptable Use Policy â€” AUP: the organizational document that defines permitted use of company IT resources. Covers internet and email acceptable use, software installation policies, personal device policies, social media conduct, and prohibited activities. All users must acknowledge and agree to the AUP before being granted system access. A splash screen at login is a common method of displaying the AUP notice and obtaining electronic acknowledgment. Violations of the AUP carry consequences ranging from warnings to termination.
---
exam_tips: PCI-DSS = payment card data. HIPAA = healthcare PHI. PII = any individually identifying data â€” governed by state breach notification laws. Know which regulation covers which data type â€” the exam presents scenarios asking you to identify the applicable regulation.

sections.title: Software Licensing
sections.content:
Software licensing is a professional responsibility that carries legal and financial consequences for non-compliance.
EULA â€” End-User License Agreement: the legal contract between the software vendor and the user. The EULA defines what the user is permitted to do with the software. Most users click through EULAs without reading them â€” but the terms govern use cases like commercial deployment, redistribution, modification, and number of installations. Violating the EULA is a breach of contract.
License types. Perpetual license: a one-time purchase that grants rights to use a specific version of the software indefinitely. Does not automatically include future versions or ongoing support. The purchased version can be used without a subscription.
Personal-use license: grants rights for use on personal devices for non-commercial purposes. Using personal-use licensed software in a business context is a license violation â€” even if you paid for the software.
Corporate-use license: designed for business and commercial use. Often per-seat â€” one license per installation â€” or volume licensed. Typically includes support, management tools, and rights to deploy on organizational devices.
Subscription license: grants access for the duration of the subscription period. When the subscription expires, access terminates. Common for cloud-based software and modern productivity suites.
Open-source licenses: software with freely available source code. License terms vary significantly. GPL â€” GNU General Public License: any derivative work must also be open-sourced under the same license. MIT License: very permissive â€” minimal restrictions on use or modification. Apache License: permissive with patent protections. Understanding which open-source license applies to software in use matters for commercial products that incorporate open-source components.
NDAs â€” Non-Disclosure Agreements: legal contracts protecting confidential information. A unilateral NDA â€” one-way â€” is signed by a party receiving confidential information from another. A mutual NDA â€” MNDA â€” is signed by both parties when both share confidential information. Common in employment agreements, vendor relationships, and consulting engagements. Disclosing NDA-protected information can result in legal liability.
---
exam_tips: Using a personal-use license for commercial/business purposes is a license violation â€” even if you paid for the software. GPL = derivative works must also be open-sourced. MIT and Apache are more permissive for commercial use. EULA is the legal agreement that governs all license types.

sections.title: Incident Response And Forensics
sections.content:
When a security incident occurs, the response must follow documented procedures to preserve evidence and maintain legal standing.
Chain of custody: a documented record of who had possession of evidence, when, and why. Every person who handles evidence must be recorded in the chain of custody log. Every transfer â€” from the scene to the technician, from the technician to forensics, from forensics to legal â€” is documented with dates, times, and signatures. A broken or incomplete chain of custody can render evidence inadmissible in legal proceedings. This is critical when criminal activity may be involved.
Evidence preservation: never work on original evidence. Create a forensic image â€” a bit-for-bit copy of the original drive â€” using a write-blocker. A write-blocker is a hardware or software device that allows reading from the drive without writing anything to it. The original drive is preserved unchanged. All analysis is performed on the forensic copy. This ensures the original evidence is not altered.
Order of volatility: the order in which digital evidence must be collected is determined by how quickly it disappears. Collect the most volatile evidence first.
CPU registers and cache: the processor's current operational state. Lost the instant the processor is powered off.
RAM: random access memory contains the most actionable forensic data â€” currently running processes, active network connections, decrypted data, encryption keys, passwords, and evidence of activity that leaves no trace on disk. Lost when power is removed from the system. RAM imaging is performed on a live system using forensic tools.
Swap and page file: virtual memory stored on disk. More persistent than RAM. May contain data that was in RAM during normal operation.
Hard disk or SSD: persistent storage. Retained after power off. Can be imaged offline.
System logs: log files on disk â€” Event Viewer logs, syslog, application logs. Persistent.
Backups and archives: the least volatile â€” retained long-term in backup storage.
The practical decision: if a system is suspected of being compromised and is currently running, decide whether to collect RAM evidence before shutting down. Shutting off immediately preserves the disk state but destroys RAM contents. Leaving the system running allows RAM collection but risks the malware altering or destroying evidence. The correct approach depends on the nature of the incident and the investigation requirements.
Reporting: security incidents, policy violations, and potential crimes require reporting through appropriate channels. Policy violations and data incidents are reported to management through organizational escalation procedures. Criminal activity â€” hacking, theft, fraud â€” may require reporting to law enforcement. Know the organization's incident response plan and escalation path before an incident occurs.
---
exam_tips: Order of volatility = collect most volatile first. RAM is LOST when power is removed â€” capture it on a live system before shutting down if RAM evidence is needed. CPU registers disappear instantly at power-off. Disk and logs persist â€” collect after volatile evidence is secured.

sections.title: Environmental Controls And Disposal
sections.content:
Server room environmental conditions: IT equipment operates within defined temperature and humidity ranges.
Ideal temperature: 64 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit (18 to 24 degrees Celsius). Too hot: components fail, system crashes, and accelerated component aging. Too cold: condensation forms on components when cold equipment is moved to a warmer environment, which can cause short circuits.
Ideal humidity: 40 to 60 percent relative humidity. Too humid: corrosion of metal contacts and component degradation. Too low: increased ESD risk â€” dry air allows static charge to build up on surfaces.
Equipment placement: maintain adequate airflow around equipment. Avoid placing equipment in direct sunlight â€” heat and UV exposure damage components. Keep intake and exhaust vents clear. In rack cabinets, use hot aisle/cold aisle configurations to direct airflow efficiently.
MSDS â€” Material Safety Data Sheet â€” also called SDS (Safety Data Sheet): required documentation for handling and disposing of hazardous materials. Required by OSHA for workplace safety compliance. Contains health hazards and symptoms, first aid procedures, storage requirements, disposal procedures, and required PPE. MSDS sheets must be accessible to all employees who work with the covered materials.
Battery disposal: do not dispose of batteries in regular trash. Lithium batteries â€” found in laptops, smartphones, and tablets â€” are a fire hazard if damaged or improperly disposed of. They contain toxic materials that contaminate soil and water. Take to recycling centers, designated drop-off locations, or retailer take-back programs.
Toner disposal: do not use a regular vacuum to clean up toner spills. Toner particles are extremely fine â€” a regular vacuum exhaust will spread them into the air. Use a toner-rated vacuum with a HEPA filter. Recycle toner cartridges through manufacturer take-back programs or office supply store recycling programs. Toner contains carcinogenic particles â€” avoid inhalation.
E-waste: electronic waste must be disposed of through certified e-waste recyclers â€” not in regular trash. Electronic components contain hazardous materials including lead, mercury, cadmium, and other heavy metals. Always wipe data from devices before disposal. Obtain certificates of destruction where required.
Compressed air usage: hold the can upright â€” tilting allows liquid propellant to spray out. Use short bursts â€” extended spraying causes condensation. Work in a ventilated area. Effective for removing dust from components, fans, and vents.
---
exam_tips: Surge suppressor = NO battery backup â€” power loss = immediate device shutdown. UPS = battery backup + surge protection. Online UPS has zero switchover delay â€” equipment always runs from battery. Line-interactive is the most common choice for workstations and networking gear.

sections.title: Power Protection
sections.content:
Surge suppressor â€” also called surge protector: protects connected equipment from voltage spikes â€” sudden increases in line voltage caused by lightning, utility switching, or large motor loads. Does not provide battery backup. When utility power fails, connected equipment loses power immediately. Less expensive than UPS.
UPS â€” Uninterruptible Power Supply: provides both surge protection and battery backup. When utility power fails, the UPS battery sustains connected equipment â€” providing runtime to execute a controlled shutdown or to ride through a brief outage. Also provides line conditioning â€” filtering and smoothing the power delivered to connected equipment. Three types.
Online UPS â€” double-conversion: equipment always runs from the battery, which is continuously charged from the wall. Zero switchover time â€” there is no transition when utility power fails because the equipment was already on battery. Best protection. Most expensive. Used for servers and network infrastructure where even a millisecond interruption is unacceptable.
Line-interactive UPS: the most common type for workstations and networking equipment. Surge suppression is active at all times. When utility power fails, there is a brief switchover time â€” typically a few milliseconds â€” before battery power takes over. Good protection at moderate cost.
Standby UPS â€” offline UPS: monitors the power line and normally passes utility power directly to connected equipment. Switches to battery only when it detects a failure. Has the longest switchover delay of the three types â€” typically 10 to 20 milliseconds. Least expensive UPS type. Basic protection for equipment that can tolerate a brief power interruption.
---
exam_tips: Never use a regular vacuum on toner â€” HEPA toner-rated vacuum only. Never put lithium batteries or electronics in regular trash â€” regulated as hazardous waste. Ideal server room: 64-75Â°F, 40-60% humidity. Too dry increases ESD risk significantly.

practice_questions.q: What is the recommended temperature range for most data centers and server rooms?
options: 18-27 degrees C (64-81 degrees F) â€” ASHRAE guidelines

practice_questions.q: What device is specifically designed to protect equipment from power surges and voltage spikes, but does NOT provide battery backup?
practice_questions.explanation: A surge protector is specifically designed to absorb excess voltage from spikes and surges. A UPS also provides surge protection but its primary function is battery backup for outages. A line conditioner filters power quality issues (noise, sags). When the exam asks specifically about surge/spike pr

practice_questions.q: What does a UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) provide?
options: Battery backup power to allow proper shutdown during outages plus power conditioning

practice_questions.q: What causes a "brownout" in electrical power?
options: Temporary reduction in voltage below normal levels
Brief power spike above normal voltage

practice_questions.q: What is the purpose of hot aisle/cold aisle containment in a data center?
options: Improve cooling efficiency by directing cold air intake and hot air exhaust separately

practice_questions.q: A company wants to reduce energy consumption from desktop workstations left running overnight. Which power management configuration is most effective?
options: Enable screen savers with high-resolution graphics
Increase RAM so workstations run more efficiently
Set workstations to hibernate or power off after a defined idle period
Upgrade all hard drives to SSDs
practice_questions.explanation: Configuring workstations to hibernate or power off after idle periods dramatically reduces power consumption during unattended hours. Screen savers do not reduce power draw and may increase GPU load.

practice_questions.q: An organization is replacing 50 older laptops and wants to dispose of them responsibly. Which is the correct method?
options: Place them in general office waste recycling bins
Store them indefinitely in a storage room
Disassemble them and dispose of components in separate trash bags
Send them to a certified e-waste recycler or follow local electronic disposal regulations
practice_questions.explanation: Electronic devices contain hazardous materials including lead, mercury, and cadmium that cannot go in standard waste streams. Certified e-waste recyclers handle these materials in compliance with environmental regulations such as RCRA.

practice_questions.q: A server room experiences intermittent hardware failures. Temperature monitoring shows 85Â°F (29Â°C) during peak hours. What environmental control should be implemented?
options: Increase airflow and cooling capacity through the HVAC system
Install additional UPS units to stabilize power
Replace all spinning drives with SSDs
Add more RAM to reduce processing load
practice_questions.explanation: Servers are designed to operate at 64â€“80Â°F (18â€“27Â°C). Sustained temperatures above this range cause thermal throttling, component degradation, and hardware failures. Improving HVAC capacity directly addresses the root cause.

practice_questions.q: A used printer toner cartridge needs to be disposed of. Which method is correct?
options: Empty the toner into a trash can and recycle the shell
Return the cartridge through a manufacturer recycling program or certified toner recycler
Rinse the cartridge with water and place it in plastic recycling
Dispose of the cartridge in general office waste
practice_questions.explanation: Toner is a chemically complex powder that should not be released into general waste or the environment. Manufacturer take-back programs and certified recyclers handle toner cartridges safely.

practice_questions.q: Which program certifies that computer equipment meets specific energy efficiency standards set by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency?
practice_questions.explanation: ENERGY STAR is the EPA's voluntary certification program for computers, monitors, and other devices meeting defined energy efficiency benchmarks. RoHS restricts hazardous substances; WEEE governs e-waste in Europe; ISO 14001 is an environmental management standard.

practice_questions.q: What type of software license allows a single user to install the software on one computer?
What does EULA stand for?
options: Open-source provides the source code; freeware is free to use but source code may not be available
Freeware provides source code; open-source does not
Open-source is always free; freeware requires payment

practice_questions.q: What is PII (Personally Identifiable Information)?
options: Information that can identify a specific individual such as name, SSN, or address

practice_questions.q: What regulation protects the privacy of EU citizens data and imposes requirements on organizations handling that data?
During a PC cleanup, a technician discovers a folder containing what appears to be medical records for individuals not employed at the company. What should the technician do?
options: Delete the files immediately to protect privacy
No action is required as it is likely a backup
Encrypt the folder as a precaution
Stop work and report the discovery through the incident response process to a supervisor
practice_questions.explanation: Medical records are Protected Health Information (PHI), a sensitive data category. Discovering sensitive data outside its authorized location is a potential breach that must be reported immediately rather than handled unilaterally.

practice_questions.q: A user asks a technician to install a single-license application on five workstations because the company purchased only one license. Which issue does this create?
options: A software licensing violation constituting software piracy
A data privacy concern under GDPR
practice_questions.explanation: Installing software on more machines than permitted by the license is piracy, violating the EULA and copyright law. Organizations face significant legal and financial penalties for unlicensed software use.

practice_questions.q: A company receives software at no cost with permission to use, modify, and redistribute the source code under specific terms. Which license type applies?
practice_questions.explanation: Open source licenses (GPL, MIT, Apache) grant users the right to use, view, modify, and redistribute source code under specific conditions. OEM licenses are tied to hardware; volume licenses cover multiple installations; retail licenses are single-user commercial licenses.

practice_questions.q: An employee uses a company laptop and network storage to run a personal side business during work hours. Which policy does this most directly violate?
practice_questions.explanation: An AUP defines what company resources may be used for. Running a personal business on company equipment and storage is a typical AUP violation, using company resources for unauthorized personal gain.

practice_questions.q: A company doing business with EU customers must comply with regulations governing personal data collection, storage, and the right to erasure. Which regulation primarily governs these requirements?
practice_questions.explanation: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is the EU's comprehensive data privacy law granting EU residents rights over their personal data, including access, correction, and deletion. Organizations handling EU residents' data must comply regardless of where they are based.

practice_questions.q: What is HIPAA, and what obligations does it place on IT professionals who handle systems storing medical records?
options: HIPAA is a software licensing standard for healthcare applications requiring annual compliance renewal

HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) protects protected health information (PHI) — IT professionals must implement encryption, access controls, audit logging, and report breaches; violation penalties can reach millions of dollars
HIPAA only applies to doctors and nurses — IT professionals have no compliance obligations
HIPAA is a voluntary certification standard healthcare organizations can opt into for marketing purposes
practice_questions.explanation: HIPAA's Security Rule requires organizations handling electronic PHI (ePHI) to implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards including: access controls, audit controls, encryption, integrity controls, and transmission security. IT professionals designing, administering, or accessing healthcare systems must understand these requirements. A reportable breach can result in significant fines and reputational damage.
